column1: Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes is a {{c1::dirty read}}.
column2:
For example, one transaction reads a new balance before its writer commits. If the writer rolls back, the value the reader saw never became committed data.
Review source

column1: Within a transaction, rereading a row and seeing another transaction's committed change is a {{c1::nonrepeatable read}}.
column2:
The two reads target the same row, but another transaction commits a change between them. The second read can see a different value even though the reader did not change it.
Review source

column1: If another transaction inserts and commits a matching row, a repeated search can show {{c1::phantom reads}}.
column2:
The first search finds one matching row, and another transaction inserts a second match and commits. The same search then finds two rows. The difference is in which rows match, not necessarily their values.
Review source

column1: SQL Server's default session isolation level is {{c1::READ COMMITTED}}.
column2:
READ COMMITTED prevents reading uncommitted changes. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT determines whether the engine uses shared data locks or committed row versions for ordinary reads at that isolation level.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Fabric, READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT defaults to {{c1::ON}}.
column2:
With the option on, each ordinary READ COMMITTED statement sees a committed view from its start. The session isolation level is still READ COMMITTED. This is not a transaction-wide SNAPSHOT.
Review source

column1: Enable SNAPSHOT transactions in StudyDB with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE StudyDB SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON;}}
column2:
The database option permits transactions to use SNAPSHOT. The session still needs to request SNAPSHOT explicitly. Existing sessions do not switch to that isolation level just because the database permits it.
Review source

column1: Before starting a SNAPSHOT transaction, select the session level with {{c1::SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;}}
column2:
This statement selects SNAPSHOT for the session. The database must permit it through ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION. Once the transaction first accesses data, later reads use the same snapshot plus its own changes.
Review source

column1: Enable RCSI for StudyDB with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE StudyDB SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;}}
column2:
This database option changes ordinary READ COMMITTED reads to use row versions. Other connections must be closed during the change. It does not select SNAPSHOT as the session isolation level.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Fabric, optimized locking is {{c1::always enabled}}.
column2:
These managed platforms provide optimized locking without a per-database enablement step. SQL Server 2025 requires explicit database enablement, so do not assume the managed default applies to it.
Review source

column1: Optimized locking depends on the recovery feature {{c1::accelerated database recovery (ADR)}}.
column2:
Accelerated database recovery (ADR) maintains persistent row versions that optimized locking depends on. That prerequisite is already present in Azure SQL Database. Lock after qualification also needs RCSI for ordinary READ COMMITTED use.
Review source

column1: Under optimized locking at READ COMMITTED, an exclusive {{c1::transaction ID (TID)}} lock protects modifications until transaction end.
column2:
The writer holds the exclusive transaction ID lock while the transaction remains open. This replaces many long-held data locks in this configuration and lowers the memory needed to track locks.
Review source

column1: With a unique ProductID, reserve one available unit: UPDATE dbo.Products SET StockCount = StockCount - 1 WHERE ProductID = @ProductID AND {{c1::StockCount > 0}};
column2:
With one unit left, this condition lets the first successful update reduce stock to zero. A competing update cannot also reserve that unit. Use the affected-row count before creating the order in the same transaction.
Review source
